title: Chapter 61 – The Door Answers
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The letter has three seals, and his father opens them one at a time, like a man taking apart a trap.

They sit at the long table in the study, in the pale light of the first cold morning, with the shutters half open and a pot of millet going cold between them. Wenyuan has not touched his bowl. He has laid the envelope in front of him, a long white one, heavy and cream-colored and faintly scented, as expensive things are scented, and he is slitting the wax with the point of a small bone knife. The first seal is blue. It is the Outer Court's own, a crane with a scroll. The second is green, and bears a character Jian does not know. The third is plain gray, and is stamped with a single small thumbprint.

Cheng Yun, he thinks.

His mother stands at the window, with her arms crossed and her back to the room. She has not said a word since the messenger left. She has only looked at the envelope, once, as one looks at a snake in the grass, and then looked away.

Wenyuan unfolds the paper. It is a single sheet, closely written, in a hand that is square and black and quite without ornament. He reads it through once, slowly, with his lips pressed together. Then he sets it down and reads it again. When he is done, he lays both palms flat on the table, and for a long time he does not look up.

"Well?" says Qinghe, to the window.

"It is from the Arbiter."

"I assumed."

"It is a ruling." The Patriarch's voice is level. "It says that the Court has examined the matter of the Garden under the hill, under the ninth section of the Founder's Precept. It says that the Garden is a minor remnant of the Founder's work, of no strategic value, and incapable of sustaining a sect. It says that the Court, in its wisdom, will not take it into custody." A breath. "It will hold it in trust. In the name of the Lin clan. For ten years."

Qinghe turns. "And after ten?"

"It will review the matter."

"That is a short leash."

"It is the longest the Court has ever given." Wenyuan's mouth twists. "I do not think Shen Wuye is a man who gives much. I think this cost him something."

"And the second page?"

He looks at her. Then he looks, for the first time, at his son.

"The second page," he says, "is about you."

* * *

It is not a long paragraph. It is eleven lines, in the same square hand, and Jian reads it upside down, across the table, before his father has finished turning the sheet.

In the matter of Lin Jian, son of Lin Wenyuan, aged ten years.

The Court has observed that the said Lin Jian is a five-element child of the eighth stage, and has been so recorded by the Sect's own Mirror, in the presence of the Arbiter and an Inspector. The Court has further observed that he is the bearer of a Seed, of a school not hitherto known to the Sect. The Court holds that such a child, left unregistered, is a danger to himself and to the clan which shelters him.

It is therefore ordered that the said Lin Jian shall be entered on the roll of the Outer Court, as an Outer Sect disciple of the lowest rank, and shall present himself for instruction at the Spring Register of the coming year, in the company of the Inspector, in the fifth month.

This is not a request.

It is, however, a courtesy. The Court is aware that the child has done a service. The Court will remember it.

Shen Wuye.

He reads it twice. Then he looks up, at the long still faces of his father and mother, and finds that he is not surprised.

"They will take him," says Qinghe. It is not a question.

"They will register him."

"It is the same word, Wenyuan."

"It is not." The Patriarch's voice is quiet, and firm. "A boy on the roll of the Outer Court cannot be taken by the Blood Shadow without a writ. He cannot be taken by Red Ridge, or by any clan. He is under the Sect's hand. He is protected." He closes his eyes. "It is what I asked, in my letter. It is not the thing I wanted. It is the thing that was possible."

"He is ten."

"He is the youngest eighth-stage the Court has seen in six hundred years." Wenyuan opens his eyes. They are dry, and quite steady, and the saddest that Jian has ever seen. "He is not a child any more. I have known it for months. I thought it was a thing I could hold off, if I did not look. It is not."

Qinghe does not answer. She stands with her arms crossed and her face to the light, quite rigid, and after a long moment Jian sees that her shoulders are shaking.

"Mother," he says.

"Do not."

"I—"

"Do not, Jian." She turns. Her eyes are bright and furious. "Do not say you are sorry. Do not say you will be careful. I have had nine months of careful." Her voice cracks. "I should like, for one morning, to be permitted to be angry at a letter."

"Yes, Mother."

"Good."

She crosses the room in three strides and puts her arms round him, hard, and holds on. She smells of herbs, and woodsmoke, and a faint warm sweetness that he has known for as long as he has known anything. He stands quite still, with his face in her shoulder, and Pebble on his own, and does not try to speak.

Over her head, he meets his father's eyes. Wenyuan nods, once, slightly.

It is all right, the nod says. It will be all right.

It will not, thinks Jian. But it will be something.

* * *

There is a third page. He finds it last.

It has been folded small, and tucked behind the first, so that his father almost missed it. It is a scrap of coarse brown paper, the kind used for wrapping, and the hand on it is ragged and hasty, the strokes slanting down to the right, as of a man writing on his knee.

Jian.

They are going to want to see the Seed. I do not know how I know it. I have been in the Outer Court four months, and I have heard things. The Elders say there was a five-element child at the Founder's Gate six hundred years ago, and that no one has ever spoken of what became of him.

Come. But do not let them have it. Do not let them touch it. Say it is nothing. Say it is a pill.

I am a first-ranker now. They say I will be a second by spring. I have a room with a window. It looks over the Gate Trial, and I have been counting the steps. There are forty. There is a lock at the fortieth, and I have stood in front of it every night, and I have never once wanted to see what is behind it so much as I want to see you.

Feng.

P.S. Zhao Yao has a broken arm. It is the funniest thing I have ever seen.

He reads it three times, in the thin light, with his lips moving. He is smiling. He finds that his eyes are wet.

A lock at the fortieth.

It is the thing he has stared at for two years. It is the thing that the plate under the Orchard is a cousin of. And his brother, in a room with a window, has been standing in front of it every night, with a cold brown wrapper on his knee, counting.

We are going to open it, he thinks. We are going to open it together.

* * *

His father finds him on the east wing roof in the afternoon.

Wenyuan climbs the ladder slowly, with one hand on the rail, like a man much older. He sits on the tiles beside his son, a little apart, and for a while neither of them speaks. Below them the yard is full of the small ordinary sounds of a clan that has not yet decided how to feel: a hammer, a cart, a woman calling a child in to wash.

"Spring Register," says Wenyuan at last. "The fifth month. That is seven months."

"Yes, Father."

"I have been counting what we can do with seven months." He rubs his jaw. "Hu has agreed to stay. He will train the guards, and the Keepers, and anyone who will stand still. Wenqing will take the ledgers. Elder Zhong has asked to be allowed to teach the children their letters, and I have said yes, and I do not know whether I was right." A short, dry breath. "Your mother wishes to teach you a great many things before you go. She has made a list. It is four pages."

"What is on it?"

"Everything. How to mend a cloak. How to tell a liar from a man who is only nervous. How to write home." He pauses. "It does not say how to come back. I think she has left that line blank on purpose."

Jian looks at his hands. They are small hands. They are ten years old, and cracked across the knuckles, and there is a faint silver shimmer under the skin of the right palm that was not there a month ago.

"I will come back," he says.

"I know you will." Wenyuan does not look at him. "That is not what I am afraid of."

"What are you afraid of?"

The Patriarch is quiet for a long time. The wind lifts the loose end of his sleeve.

"That you will come back and I will not be the one who is in charge of you," he says. "That you will come back and be theirs. That there will be a day when I look at you across a table and see the Court looking out." He shakes his head. "It is a foolish thing. Forget I said it."

"No," says Jian.

He puts out his hand. After a moment, awkwardly, as though it were a thing he had never done, Wenyuan takes it. His palm is hard and dry, and warm, and it closes round Jian's whole fist.

"I will not forget it," says Jian. "I will not forget any of it."

That, he thinks, is the only promise I can keep.

* * *

He goes down to the Garden at dusk.

He does not tell anyone. He has not told anyone anything, in the last month, that he could help. He slips out of the hall by the back stair, and down through the cellar, and into the old seam, with Pebble on his shoulder and a lantern in his hand, and the cold green light takes him as it has taken him a hundred times. It is a thing he has learned to do without thought. He steps in, and the world folds, and he is on the moss.

It is quiet. The Wardens are in their ring. The pool glimmers. A few of the guards, the clan's new Keepers of the Garden, are sitting at the far end of the avenue, among the herb beds, playing at dice by a hooded lamp. They look up, as he passes, and nod. He nods back. It is a thing he has not yet grown used to, being nodded at.

Where are we going? says Pebble, from his shoulder.

I do not know.

That is a lie.

A little.

Hmm. She is quiet a moment. Her small cold nose is against his ear. The plate, she says. You are going to the plate.

Yes.

It is not asleep.

He stops. He has been walking, he finds, quite without meaning to, toward the terrace, past the pool and the dim ring of Wardens, up the three black steps. He stands at the top, in the lantern's circle, and looks at the great dull disc of black metal. It lies as it has lain for a month, with its long clean crack running through it from rim to rim.

It has been humming, says Pebble. Since the day you turned your hand. Very quietly. Like a large animal, who is not yet awake and is thinking of it.

Why did you not tell me?

I thought you knew.

He laughs, a little, under his breath. He kneels. He holds the lantern close to the black metal, and the light slides over it, over the cracks and the fine fine lines, and he sees something he has not seen before.

There is a mark in the center.

It is a small one. It lies in the heart of the disc, where the lines run together, a faint pale smudge on the dull black, about the size of his own hand. At first he takes it for a flaw. Then he lifts the lantern, and tilts it, and understands.

It is a handprint.

It is his. It is the print of the palm that he laid, a month ago, in a red garden, on the cold metal, and turned. It has sunk into the plate, as a hand sinks into wet clay, and dried there. He can see the lines. The long crease at the heel of the thumb. The three small scars across the base of the fingers, where a Seam Needle's thread has bitten. And over it all, faint and silver and exact, a ring of tiny characters, in Coral Gate script, that were not there before.

It has taken my name, he thinks.

Of course it has, says Pebble, patiently. You are the gardener.

* * *

She does it herself.

He does not ask. He does not even think to. She slides from his shoulder, slowly, down his arm, and onto the black metal, and walks across it, small and bare and pale, with her round body swaying and her tail dragging over the crack. She goes to the middle. She stops at the print. She looks at it for a long time with her head cocked, as she looks at everything, with the grave absorbed attention of a creature that has smelled a thing for the first time.

Then she lifts one small hand, and lays it, lightly, in the middle of his palm.

Mother, says Pebble.

It is the faintest thing he has ever heard. It is not a word. It is a feeling, a thin warm wave of such enormous, such helpless longing that his breath stops in his chest. He has felt it before. He felt it in the quarry, in the red dark, on the first night. It is the thing she says when she thinks that nobody is listening.

The plate sings.

It is not a loud note. It is a low, slow, round tone, like the call of a large bell at the bottom of the sea, and it goes through the Garden like a wave through water. The pool stirs. The Wardens lift their heads. The lantern flickers, and the light on the black metal turns, all at once, from gold to green.

The crack widens.

He sees it happen. It is not a break, but an opening, like the parting of a pair of great gray lips. The two halves of the plate slide apart, with a long soft grinding whisper, and under them, in the dark, there is a faint pale glow. Not red. Not green. It is the color of a candle seen through paper. It comes up in a thin ring, and it lights the underside of the Warden's face, and the cold bare stone of the terrace, and the pale small shape of a pangolin standing on the edge of a hole in the world.

There is a stair.

It goes down. It is a narrow spiral stair of pale gray stone, wide enough for one, with a rail of black iron worn smooth by hands. It turns once, twice, and disappears. A cold dry air comes up it, smelling of dust and old paper and something he cannot name, a clean faint sweetness, like the smell of a room in which a long time has passed without anyone entering.

One, says the interface, in the corner of his eye. It is a single plain line. One stair.

He does not know what it means. He looks at the count, and at the stair, and at the little pale creature on the lip of the hole, and a thin cold hand closes round his heart.

One, he thinks. One stair. And how many more?

I do not know, says Pebble. But I think it is polite. I think it will only show us one at a time.

* * *

He takes the stair alone.

It is a thing that he will think about, afterward, for a long time. He should have called his father. He should have told the Keepers, or Hu, or woken the Wardens, or at the very least left a note. He does none of those things. He puts the lantern in his left hand, and Pebble on his shoulder, and sets his right on the black rail, and goes down into the dark, one step at a time, counting.

Eleven. Twelve.

The stair turns. The walls are close and bare, and cold to the touch. There is no dust. There is no sound but the soft scuff of his own boots and the thin tick of his heart. He has the odd sense, as he goes, of being expected: of every step having been laid, not by a workman, but by a host, and the whole of the narrow spiral swept and made ready, for a long time, against a particular footfall.

Thirty-nine. Forty.

It ends.

It opens, without warning, onto a small round chamber, no more than ten paces across, with a floor of white stone and a low domed roof, and in the middle of it, on a pedestal of black glass, there is a thing he knows.

He stops on the threshold. His breath goes out of him in a thin hard rush. He puts a hand on the wall, and for a moment the whole round room swims.

It is a cradle.

It is a shallow bowl of dull silver, a foot across, with a long slender curve like the neck of a swan rising from one side of it, and a ring of small glassy studs set round the rim. It is a thing of no great beauty. It is plain, and slightly worn, and quite cold. It rests on its black pedestal, in the pale light, with a faint slow pulse along its curve, a rhythm that is not a light but a shape, like the slow breath of a sleeper.

He makes himself look at the rest of the room before he looks at the cradle again. It is a habit, and a good one. There is no second door. The walls are bare white stone, close and smooth, without a seam. A ring of characters has been cut into the floor round the pedestal, in the same Coral Gate script as the print above, small and precise, and he kneels at the edge of it with the lantern and reads, moving his lips.

For the one who tends.

This room holds what was carried out of the first world. It is not a weapon. It is not a treasure. It is a key that was cut to fit a hand, and it will not turn for any other.

Do not bring a second person here. Do not bring a second light.

He glances at Pebble on his shoulder, and at the single lantern in his hand. I am not a person, she says, very small. I am the Garden's. I think it knows the difference. The lantern is the only light he carries, and the wall says nothing more. He decides to believe her, and decides to remember that he did.

What you take from this room, you will not be able to put back.

He rereads the last line. A faint chill crawls up his spine.

Every advantage has a cost, he thinks. It is the oldest rule I know. I did not expect to find it carved in stone.

It is polite, says Pebble, from his shoulder, small. It tells you the price before you reach for the cup.

That is not politeness. That is a trap that wants you to be certain.

Hmm. Is there a difference?

He does not answer. He stands, slowly, with his knees aching, and turns back to the pedestal.

He has seen it before.

He has not seen it with his eyes. He has seen it with the mind he had before, in another life, in a bright white room full of the smell of ozone, in the long middle hours of a night: on a bench, under a lamp, with a ring of small glassy studs set round the rim of a silver bowl, and a slender curved neck rising from the side. It is the thing he carried in his hands to the table on the last day. It is the coil.

ARK-7.

The words come to him from a long way off. They are not in any voice. They are not his. They are simply there, as a name is there, at the back of the tongue.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Component recognized: SCANNER COIL (primary).
Status: dormant. Dock: AVAILABLE.
Integration will connect Interface to its housing.
Integration will NOT be reversible.
Integration will CHANGE the Interface.
Note: This is not Fragment 3.
Proceed? [Y/N]
```

Not Fragment 3, he thinks.

He has been hunting the third fragment for two years. It is the missing piece of the thing in his head, the one the interface refuses to name, and every time he has believed himself close it has slid away. He had assumed, without ever quite saying so, that the Garden would end the hunt. Instead it has laid a different piece on a pedestal, and warned him that taking it would change the whole.

Change it how? he asks the panel, silently, with all the care he can muster.

The panel does not answer. It never does, to questions. It states, and waits.

He counts the costs as he would count coins. If he refuses, the cradle stays here, dormant, under a hill that the Court now holds in trust for ten years. He will go to the Outer Court in seven months with Level 3 and a half-finished Seed and no more. If he accepts, he gives up something he cannot see, to gain something he cannot measure, in a room he was told not to share.

Seven months, he thinks. I have seven months to decide.

He stands in the doorway with the lantern shaking in his hand, and the little round room breathing round him, and the thing on its pedestal pulsing slowly, slowly, as if it knew his name. A long way above him, through ninety paces of stone, a few small sounds are coming down the stair: the clink of dice, a faint laugh, the soft footfall of a Warden. It is the ordinary noise of a hill at the end of a day.

One stair, he thinks. And a cradle shaped like the thing in my head.

He does not move. He does not press the panel. He stands still, in the pale light, with his heart going like a drum and the whole of the long dark corridor of his two lives opening out behind him, and ahead, one small step further on, a single bright question with two letters on it.

Not yet, thinks Jian.

It is the interface's own phrase. He had not known he would borrow it.

Not yet. But soon.

And on the pedestal, in the pale round room, the cradle gives a long slow pulse, like a sleeper turning in a dream, and one of the small glassy studs on its rim, softly, begins to glow.
